content: 1. The impact of hepatic impairment on the pharmacokinetics of tranexamic acid has not been studied. Only a small percentage of an oral dose (1% as a dicarboxylic acid and 0.5% as an acetylated metabolite) is metabolized and excreted. Therefore, no dose adjustment is necessary for patients with hepatic impairment. 2. No formal drug-drug interaction studies have been conducted with tranexamic acid. However, due to its antifibrinolytic properties, concurrent use of tranexamic acid with combination hormonal contraceptives is contraindicated as it may exacerbate the already increased thrombotic risk associated with these contraceptives. 3. Tranexamic acid is not recommended for patients receiving Factor IX complex concentrates or anti-inhibitor coagulant concentrates due to the potential for an increased risk of thrombosis. 4. Concomitant use of tranexamic acid with tissue plasminogen activators may reduce the efficacy of both agents. Caution is advised if a patient on tranexamic acid therapy requires tissue plasminogen activators. 5. In a study involving 28 patients with acute promyelocytic leukemia, those treated with all-trans retinoic acid (oral tretinoin) and tranexamic acid experienced a high mortality rate, with thrombotic complications being the primary cause of death in most cases. The procoagulant effects of all-trans retinoic acid may be amplified by tranexamic acid. Caution is advised when prescribing tranexamic acid to such patients. 6. Carcinogenicity studies in male mice at doses up to six times the recommended human dose (3900 mg/day) showed an increased incidence of leukemia, potentially related to treatment. Female mice were not included in these studies. Hyperplasia and neoplastic changes in the biliary tract were observed in one strain of rats at doses exceeding the maximum tolerated dose for 22 months, but subsequent studies in a different rat strain did not replicate these findings. 7. Tranexamic acid was not found to be mutagenic or clastogenic in in vitro bacterial reverse mutation assays (Ames test), in vitro chromosome aberration tests in Chinese hamster cells, or in in vivo chromosome aberration tests in mice and rats. 8. Reproductive studies in mice, rats, and rabbits did not show evidence of impaired fertility or adverse effects on fetal development due to tranexamic acid. In a rat embryofetal developmental toxicity study, no adverse effects were observed when tranexamic acid was administered during organogenesis at doses up to four times the recommended human dose. Similarly, no adverse effects on pup viability, growth, or development were observed in a perinatal-postnatal study in rats. 9. In a 9-month toxicology study in dogs, tranexamic acid administered in food at doses up to six times the recommended human dose caused reversible ocular effects, including reddening and gelatinous discharge from the eyes. Histopathological examinations revealed no retinal alterations. However, in other studies, focal retinal degeneration was observed in cats, dogs, and rats at doses 6-40 times the usual human dose. 10. The efficacy and safety of tranexamic acid for treating heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) were demonstrated in randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies. HMB was defined as an average menstrual blood loss (MBL) of ≥80 mL, assessed by alkaline hematin analysis. Subjects were aged 18-49 years, with a mean age of 40 years, and had a history of HMB for approximately 10 years. About 40% of subjects had fibroids, and the majority were Caucasian. 11. The 1950 mg/day dose did not meet the criteria for clinical success.
